Lead is listed with MCL TT (treatment technique) rather than a numeric MCL in the 2018 EPA table; not loaded.
EPA lists Mercury (inorganic) 0.002 mg/L, but the bulk-ingest controlled vocabulary permits tHg or MeHg only; not loaded as tHg because that would broaden the stated species.
EPA Secondary Drinking Water Regulations list aluminum as a range, 0.05 to 0.2 mg/L; not loaded as a point value.
EPA lists uranium MCL 0.03 mg/L, but U is outside the regulatory_limits.csv metal_species vocabulary in the bulk-ingest prompt; documented on the regulation page and not loaded.

WHO does not establish a formal aluminium guideline value; it gives practicable operational levels of 0.1 mg/L or less in large facilities and 0.2 mg/L or less in small facilities, not loaded as a maximum contaminant level.
WHO lists 0.006 mg/L for inorganic mercury, but the bulk-ingest controlled vocabulary permits tHg or MeHg only; not loaded as tHg because that would broaden the stated species.
WHO lists uranium 0.03 mg/L, but U is outside the regulatory_limits.csv metal_species vocabulary in the bulk-ingest prompt; documented on the regulation page and not loaded.

Codex CXS 227-2001 section 3.2.1 requires packaged waters to comply with the health-related requirements of the most recent WHO Guidelines for Drinking-water Quality but does not list metal-specific numeric limits; companion WHO rows are handled separately.

The Federal Register notice announces availability of final FDA guidance and a supporting document for lead in candy likely to be consumed frequently by small children, but the PDF text does not print the numeric recommended maximum level; do not load a value from title/context alone.

21 CFR part 109 defines FDA tolerances, regulatory limits, and action levels and includes numeric PCB tolerances, but PCBs are outside the regulatory_limits.csv metal_species vocabulary; the lead-related decorative-ceramicware text is warning/labeling language without a numeric Pb food limit.

Maryland Chapter 954 (Rudy's Law) requires baby-food testing/disclosure and prohibits sale above limits established by FDA, but it does not set its own numeric Pb, As, Cd, or Hg limits; existing FDA rows remain the numeric companions.

Codex CXS 156-1987 sections 5 (older infants) and 5 (young-child drinks/products) require covered products to comply with maximum levels in CXS 193-1995, but this PDF does not set its own Pb/Cd/As/Hg/Sn numeric contaminant values; companion CXS 193 rows are handled separately.

Codex CXS 72-1981 section 5 requires infant formula to comply with maximum levels in CXS 193-1995, but this PDF does not set its own heavy-metal contaminant values; chromium mentions are nutritional/mineral composition context, not contaminant maximum levels.

The guide explains EU market-access rules for foods containing contaminants and points to Regulation (EU) 2023/915 and related official-controls instruments for actual maximum levels; it does not itself set metal-specific numeric limits.

The manifest lists Cd only, but the PDF Annex section 3 is a full Albanian-language food-contaminant schedule covering Pb, Cd, Hg, inorganic/total arsenic, and inorganic tin across many commodity rows. Skipped in this pass rather than partially loading Cd and silently dropping the rest; needs a dedicated full-table translation/transcription pass.

California AB 899 requires baby-food manufacturers to test final baby food products for arsenic, cadmium, lead, and mercury and disclose results, but it does not set California numeric product limits. The 6 ug/kg laboratory-proficiency language is a method/proficiency criterion, not a food contaminant limit; FDA action levels or tolerances remain the numeric companions.
Schedule Four method-performance criteria mention inorganic tin LOD/LOQ, but Table 1 does not set a tin maximum residue limit; no Sn row loaded from this PDF.

The manifest filename identifies NC 493:2008 metal contaminants, but the PDF text is NC 877:2012 wheat flour specifications. Section 6.1 quotes only two NC 493 processed-cereal values, 0.1 mg/kg Pb and 0.1 mg/kg Cd, which were loaded for wheat flour/processed cereals; the full NC 493 contaminant table is not present and needs the primary standard.

Cadmium section rows 12.14-12.15 repeat natural mineral water 0.001 mg/kg and food-grade salt 0.1 mg/kg after cadmium water/salt rows 12.12-12.13 and duplicate mercury row values 10.1-10.2; skipped as unresolved source-internal conflict pending legal/errata review.

The local PDF is Appendix/Annex table 1 only and contains routeable metal values but no authority, parent instrument title, amendment history, or row-level effective dates. The official Taiwan FDA parent page identifies the Sanitation Standard for Contaminants and Toxins in Food and lists multiple amendment effective dates, including 2024-07-01 and 2026-01-01, but this annex-only PDF does not map which metal rows changed under which amendment. Deferred for a dedicated parent-instrument join rather than loading one blended effective date.

The local Cap. 132AF PDF is the Harmful Substances in Food Regulations verified copy last updated 2023-12-01. Schedule 1 contains veterinary-drug residues, aflatoxins, benzo[a]pyrene, erucic acid, glycidyl esters, melamine, patulin, and 3-MCPD, but the extracted Schedule 1 does not set numeric limits for the HMI metal species despite the manifest filename. No regulatory_limits.csv metal rows loaded from this file.

The consolidated Food Regulations 1985 PDF includes Regulation 38, which prohibits sale/import of foods exceeding metal-contaminant levels in Tables I and IA-IE of the Fourteenth Schedule, but the local text/PDF does not include the Fourteenth Schedule tables with the numeric metal limits. Deferred until the schedule tables are available; no regulatory_limits.csv rows loaded from this parent-only text.

Tenth Schedule item (b)(4)(a) covers chemicals used as ingredients or in food processing for which the British Pharmacopoeia or British Pharmaceutical Codex specifies a limit, but the Singapore PDF cross-references the current B.P. or B.P.C. limit rather than stating one numeric arsenic/lead value. The adjacent 'other chemicals' row was loaded; this cross-reference row was not.

England SI 2013/2196 executes and enforces Commission Regulation (EC) No 1881/2006 and Regulation (EC) No 124/2009. It creates offences, enforcement authorities, and sampling/analysis references, but it does not state independent metal-specific numeric maximum levels; the existing EC 1881/2006 source and regulation pages remain the numeric companions.

Executive Decree No. 14-366 of 15 December 2014 sets the general conditions for tolerated contaminants in food and states that contaminant lists and maximum residue limits are fixed by ministerial order. This gazette issue does not include metal-specific numeric food maximum levels for Pb, Cd, As, Hg, Sn, Cr, Al, Ni, or Sb; no regulatory_limits.csv rows loaded.

Joint Resolution 10/2026 incorporates MERCOSUR GMC Resolution 13/24 on the definition of contaminant in food into Article 6 of the Argentine Food Code. The PDF contains definitions and incorporation language only; it does not set metal-specific numeric food maximum levels. No regulatory_limits.csv rows loaded.

Manifest reports 16 pages but zero text characters for the sample, indicating an image-only or otherwise unextractable draft PDF. The bulk-ingest prompt forbids OCR guessing for near-zero text extraction, so no numeric contaminant rows were loaded.

SENASAG Administrative Resolution 121/2017 approves a national surveillance and control program for chemical residues and contaminants in livestock-origin foods. The program lists heavy metals (mercury, arsenic, lead, cadmium, other metals), matrices, and AAS methods, but section 11.2.5 adopts Codex, EU Directive 96/23/EC, EPA, or manufacturer references for limits rather than stating Bolivia-specific numeric metal maximum levels. No regulatory_limits.csv rows loaded.

ANVISA IN no. 160/2022 Article 6 expressly revokes IN no. 88/2021. The 2021 metals table is therefore not loaded into regulatory_limits.csv as an active Brazil standards-lookup source; use the active IN 160/2022 framework and amendments instead.

The manifest PDF is the original 2022 IN 160 text, but existing Brazil infant-food rows in regulatory_limits.csv already incorporate later IN 351/2025 amendments for lead. Loading the original table wholesale would reintroduce superseded values and duplicate current rows; deferred for a dedicated consolidated IN 160 + amendment reconciliation pass.

Government Notice 990 of 6 September 2016 is a proposed regulation: the Minister states an intent to make the regulations, invites comments within three months, and says the regulations come into operation three months after publication of the final Regulations. No active maximum-level rows loaded from this draft notice.

The 27 November 2019 MAFF slide deck summarizes Japan's food-safety legal system and risk management of contaminants. It states that MHLW sets maximum levels for Cd and methylmercury, but it does not state commodity-specific numeric metal limits; no regulatory_limits.csv rows loaded from this context deck.

The Matsne PDF is a Georgian-language technical regulation approved by Government Resolution No. 127 of 25 April 2025, generally effective 2026-06-01 with selected subpoints delayed to 2028-07-01. The metal annex contains routeable Pb, Cd, Hg, As, and inorganic Sn rows, but product scopes and delayed-effective-date subpoints require a dedicated Georgian legal-table translation/transcription pass; no regulatory_limits.csv rows loaded in this batch.

The Fiji Food Safety Regulations 2009 also set numeric limits for copper, iron, barium, borate, manganese, selenium, and other non-HMI contaminants, but those species are outside the regulatory_limits.csv controlled vocabulary in the bulk-ingest prompt; only Pb, Cd, tAs, tHg, Sn, and Cr-total rows were loaded.

The Food Safety and Standards (Contaminants, toxins and Residues) Second Amendment Regulations, 2017 add a hydrocyanic-acid limit for sago, cassava flour, tapioca flour, manihot flour, and their products. The amendment does not set numeric limits for any regulatory_limits.csv metal species; no rows loaded.

The Food Safety and Standards (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues) First Amendment Regulations, 2024 amend ochratoxin A, deoxynivalenol, antibiotic, and veterinary-drug residue provisions. The inspected text does not amend metal-contaminant maximum levels for Pb, Cd, As, Hg, Sn, Al, Ni, Cr, or Sb; no regulatory_limits.csv rows loaded.

The Food Safety and Standards (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues) Amendment Regulations, 2026 were published on 19 May 2026 but state that they come into force on 1 December 2026. The metal-contaminants change adds an inorganic-arsenic note for fish oils and commodity-wording substitutions, but the instrument is future-effective as of 2026-08-06; no current active regulatory_limits.csv rows loaded from this file in this batch.

Australia New Zealand Food Standards Code Standard 1.4.1 sets the operative rule that contaminants listed in Schedule 19 must not exceed the corresponding Schedule 19 amount, but this parent standard does not print the metal-contaminant numeric table itself. The existing FSANZ Schedule 19 source and regulation page remain the numeric companion; no duplicate rows loaded from the parent standard.

EFSA's 2008 Scientific Opinion on safety of aluminium from dietary intake is a risk-assessment opinion requested by the European Commission. It discusses dietary exposure, toxicology, and tolerable intake, but it is not a binding maximum-level regulation and does not set commodity-specific legal metal limits for regulatory_limits.csv.

EFSA's Scientific Opinion on Arsenic in Food is a CONTAM Panel risk assessment using occurrence and exposure data. It does not create legal food maximum levels; EU maximum levels are handled through the EU contaminant regulations rather than this opinion.

EFSA's 2009 Scientific Opinion on cadmium in food is a risk-assessment opinion and exposure assessment. It references maximum levels where relevant but does not itself set binding commodity-specific legal limits; no regulatory_limits.csv rows loaded.

EFSA's Scientific Opinion on Lead in Food is a toxicological and dietary-exposure risk assessment. It withdraws/reevaluates health-based guidance context but does not set legal commodity maximum levels; no regulatory_limits.csv rows loaded.

EFSA's 2020 update of the risk assessment of nickel in food and drinking water establishes toxicological reference points and exposure conclusions, not a binding maximum-level schedule. EU nickel maximum levels are handled through EU regulations; no regulatory_limits.csv rows loaded from this opinion.

The consolidated Canada Food and Drug Regulations define and incorporate the List of Contaminants and Other Adulterating Substances in Foods, as amended from time to time, but the 905-page local PDF does not print the current metal-contaminant maximum-level list. Existing Canada contaminant rows are sourced to Health Canada list/notice materials rather than this parent regulations compilation; no duplicate rows loaded.

The Article 4 general processed foods excerpt contains one generic 'Heavy metals (mg/kg): Not more than 10' specification for edible butterfat-processed products or sugar processed products, but it does not identify Pb, Cd, As, Hg, Sn, Cr, Ni, Al, or any other controlled metal_species. The existing Korea Food Code Art5 heavy-metal page remains the numeric companion.

The infant/child foods excerpt defines foods labelled for infants and young children and points manufacturing to the common food standards and contaminant criteria, but the local two-page PDF contains microbiological and sodium criteria and no numeric HMI metal limits. No regulatory_limits.csv rows loaded from this companion excerpt.

The base Food Safety and Standards (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues) Regulations, 2011 contain an older metal-contaminants table, but later FSSAI amendments substitute sub-regulation 2.1.1. The base table was not loaded as a current active source because existing India rows already include later FSSAI amendment evidence.

The Food Safety and Standards (Contaminants, Toxins and Residues) Amendment Regulations, 2020 substitute the entire metal-contaminants sub-regulation 2.1.1 and contain a full routeable table for Pb, As, Sn, Cd, Hg, MeHg, Cr, and Ni. Existing India rows from older FSSAI instruments would need to be retired or replaced before this table is loaded, so it was deferred for a dedicated FSSAI consolidation pass rather than appending conflicting active values.

Japan's 2008 foodstuffs standards translation states that soft drink beverages and powdered drink beverages must not contain detectable arsenic, lead, or cadmium. The tin 150.0 ppm rows were loaded, but the non-detect As/Pb/Cd requirements were not converted into numeric regulatory_limits.csv values because the source does not state a single numeric maximum level.

Appendix 3 of EAEU TR CU 021/2011 contains many routeable toxic-element rows for foods, but the local source is a long Russian legal table with product-scope groupings, dry/reconstituted conversion notes, freshwater/marine fish distinctions, and footnote conditions. Deferred for a dedicated Russian legal-table translation/transcription pass rather than partially loading rows and risking missed or mistranslated commodity scopes.

The Punjab Pure Food Regulations 2018 PDF contains a generic metal-contaminants table, Codex fallback rows such as 'Foods not specified / Other Foods as per Codex', color/additive impurity limits, and many later product-specific standards with separate heavy-metal rows. Loading only the obvious Appendix II table would silently drop other routeable limits and loading the Codex fallback rows would not provide single source-stated numeric values, so this source needs a dedicated full-instrument extraction pass.

Release Version 2.0 of the ASEAN Guidelines on Limits of Contaminants for Cosmetics contains the same heavy-metal limits later carried into Release Version 3.0. Version 3.0, adopted at the 30th ACSB meeting in June 2019, was loaded instead; no duplicate rows were loaded from the older v2 PDF.

BPOM Regulation No. 12 of 2019 on cosmetic contaminants is expressly revoked by Article 9 of BPOM Regulation No. 16 of 2024 when the 2024 regulation comes into force. The 2024 heavy-metal limits were loaded instead; no duplicate active rows were loaded from the superseded 2019 PDF.
